query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a friction stir processing (FSP) treatment to a W–Cu composite will generate a graded, intermixed interfacial layer that overcomes phase separation and eliminates interfacial void formation, thereby improving the composite's thermal conductivity under the heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joint components.
generation.material_initial_state: W–Cu composite with discrete/interconnected tungsten particles or ligaments embedded in a copper matrix that, in the untreated state, suffers from phase separation and interfacial void formation.
generation.intervention: Implement a single-step friction stir processing (FSP) treatment to induce localized, controlled interdiffusion between W and Cu.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied during processing at elevated temperatures (but below the melting points of Cu and W) that facilitate atomic diffusion while avoiding excessive grain growth; service conditions include high thermal flux and irradiation environments similar to those in plasma-facing component joints.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a graded, intermixed interfacial layer (core–shell type structure) between W and Cu which acts as a diffusion barrier to phase separation and void nucleation.
generation.mechanism: Friction stir processing promotes mechanical mixing and enhanced diffusion at the interface, leading to a gradual change in composition that improves interfacial bonding and structural continuity. This graded interface mitigates the formation of voids and reduces the driving force for phase separation, thereby enhancing thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The FSP-treated composite will exhibit a significantly improved thermal conductivity compared to the untreated composite, as measured under comparable heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated W–Cu composite that displays phase separation and the presence of interfacial voids, which degrade its effective thermal conductivity under service conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable for processing temperatures that allow sufficient diffusion without over-aging the microstructure, and for service conditions within the operational temperature range (approx. 180–350 °C) and irradiation environments typical for plasma-facing and cooling component interfaces in fusion reactor applications.
generation.uncertainty: The extent of interfacial mixing achievable without forming deleterious intermetallic phases is not fully established, and the behavior of the graded interface under prolonged irradiation remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples (one untreated and one processed by FSP under optimized conditions). Subject both sets to simulated service conditions including high thermal flux and controlled irradiation. Characterize the microstructure (using electron microscopy) to quantify interfacial voids and phase gradients, and perform thermal conductivity measurements pre- and post-treatment.
measurements: Quantitative thermal conductivity (e.g., using laser flash analysis)
Microstructural analysis of the interfacial region (e.g., SEM/TEM imaging for voids and composition gradients)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FSP-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity and if microstructural characterization reveals a similar degree of phase separation and interfacial voids as in the untreated samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: (1) The AlCoCrFeNi/A356 composite with a uniform particle distribution and limited interface reaction can be fabricated by friction stir processing. The core–shell structure between the HEA particles and the Al matrix in the composite can be controlled via atomic diffusion at high temperature. (2) The shell zone of the interface consists of two different layers with different microstructure and element distribution, and the formation of a gradient microstructure depends on the solution diffusion and the crystal structure of HEA alloys. (3) Microstructure and composition gradients benefit the movement of dislocation, and excellent mechanical properties can be obtained for the FSPed AMCs under an optimum solution treatment condition.

In this study, AZ91 magnesium-alloy-based metal matrix composites (MMCs) reinforced with 10 wt% of Al0.5CoCrFeNi2 high-entropy alloy (HEA) particles and SiC particles were prepared by a spark plasma sintering (SPS) process at 300 °C. The effects of reinforcements on the microstructure and mechanical properties of AZ91-based MMCs were studied. The results showed that AZ91–HEA composite consisted of α-Mg, Mg17Al12 and FCC phases. No interfacial reaction layer was observed between HEA particles and the Mg matrix. After adding HEA into AZ91, the compressive yield strength (C.Y.S) of the AZ91–HEA composite increased by 17% without degradation of failure strain. In addition, the increment in C.Y.S brought by HEA was comparable to that contributed by commonly used SiC reinforcement (15%). A relatively low porosity in the composite and enhanced interfacial bonding between the α-Mg matrix and HEA particles make HEA a potential reinforcement material in MMCs.
